title: The Unfunded Treasury Expense: The True Cost of Bank Signer Turnover
summary: Every treasury departure and hire triggers authorized signer updates across dozens of banks, each with its own documentation and timeline, creating an unfunded compliance burden that most organizations absorb without measuring.
body_markdown:
When a treasury analyst or controller resigns, the operational impact is immediately visible. Someone needs to cover daily cash positioning. Someone needs to take over payment approvals. Someone needs to run the close. What is far less visible is the signer remediation work that follows. That one departure may require authorized signer updates across 10, 20, or 50 bank accounts, each requiring separate documentation submitted to separate banks on separate timelines. Bank signer turnover is not listed in any risk register. It does not appear in any staffing model. Yet every departure and every hire triggers a compliance workstream that competes with daily treasury operations for the same limited bandwidth. Our team estimates that a single signer change across 15 bank accounts generates 20 to 40 hours of administrative work spread over 30 to 90 days.


## **Every Departure Is a Removal Project**


Removing a departing employee from bank accounts is not a single action. It is a per-bank project. One bank requires a board resolution. Another needs notarized signature cards. A third accepts changes through an online portal but requires existing signers to approve the update before it processes. Each bank operates on its own timeline, and none of them treat signer removal as urgent. The treasury team submits the paperwork and waits. During that waiting period, the former employee technically retains the authority to transact. Treasury governance depends on closing that window quickly. The banks' processes make it structurally difficult to do so.


The employee left in two weeks. The signer removal takes three months.


## **Every Hire Is an Addition Project**


The other side of bank signer turnover is equally burdensome. A new controller or treasury manager cannot execute payments, approve wires, or access bank portals until they are added as an authorized signer. That means assembling documentation packages for each bank, submitting identification, and waiting for each institution to process the addition. Until the addition clears, the new hire operates through workarounds: asking existing signers to execute on their behalf, using shared credentials that violate bank account controls, or simply waiting while time-sensitive transactions queue up.


We often see new treasury hires unable to fully perform their role for 30 to 60 days because authorized signer updates at multiple banks have not completed. That is not an onboarding gap. It is an operational constraint imposed by the banking infrastructure.


## **The Compounding Effect in High-Turnover Environments**


At organizations with stable treasury teams, signer updates are infrequent enough to absorb. At property management companies, real estate funds, and other organizations where finance staff turnover is higher, the burden compounds. Two departures and two hires in a quarter means four separate signer remediation cycles running simultaneously across the same set of banks. The treasury team managing daily operations is also managing an ongoing stream of bank paperwork that never fully resolves before the next change arrives.


- A controller departs and removal requests go out to 20 banks. Three banks have not processed the removal before the replacement starts and addition requests go out to the same 20 banks.


- A temporary gap in signer coverage on certain accounts means payment authority is concentrated in fewer people, increasing key-person risk.


- Documentation requirements differ per bank, so the team cannot use a single package for all institutions.


Turnover does not just cost you a person. It costs you months of bank administration.


## **The Cost Nobody Tracks**


Treasury leaders budget for salaries, systems, and bank fees. Nobody budgets for the administrative cost of signer turnover. Yet the hours are real: preparing documentation, coordinating with banks, following up on unprocessed requests, and tracking status across institutions. At organizations managing 30 or more bank accounts, a single turnover event can absorb the equivalent of a full week of a senior team member's time once follow-up and escalation are included. Over a year with two or three turnover events, that is a material allocation of treasury capacity that never appears in any operational metric.


## **Centralizing Signer Management Reduces the Turnover Burden**


The per-bank administrative model is the core problem. Every bank operating independently means every signer change is multiplied by the number of banking relationships. A platform like Arpari centralizes signer tracking across all banks, providing a single view of who is authorized on which accounts. When a departure occurs, the platform identifies every account affected. When a new hire joins, the required updates are visible immediately rather than discovered bank by bank. Treasury governance improves because the organization controls the tracking even when it cannot control the bank's processing speed.


## **Key Takeaways**


Bank signer turnover creates a compliance and administrative burden that most treasury teams absorb without measuring. Every departure requires removal across multiple banks. Every hire requires addition across the same banks. Both processes run on the bank's timeline, not the organization's, creating risk windows and operational gaps that persist for weeks or months. Treasury leaders and controllers should track the actual cost of signer remediation and treat it as a recurring operational expense rather than an invisible one. Centralizing authorized signer updates through a single platform reduces the per-bank coordination burden and ensures that every turnover event is managed as a complete project rather than a scattered set of individual bank requests. The people will always change. The process for managing that change should not depend on how many banks you have.
